analysis.one_liner: Lets federal agencies suspend or permanently repeal regulations during the COVID emergency without public input.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2020 with zero cosponsors, the bill never received committee action and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed every federal agency to identify regulations that 'may inhibit economic recovery' from COVID-19, and let agency heads temporarily or permanently rescind, modify, waive, or exempt businesses from them. It would let agencies skip the normal notice-and-comment process, which is the public's chance to weigh in before federal rules change. It also would have pushed agencies to go easy on enforcement against businesses that claim good-faith compliance, and barred enforcement actions against a business solely for ignoring agency guidance.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses across the economy — employers, manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and others subject to federal health, safety, environmental, consumer, and financial rules — would gain freedom from those requirements and lighter enforcement during the emergency, including the chance to have some rules rescinded permanently. The bill text emphasizes helping businesses, especially small ones, 're-open' with confidence.

how_it_helps.text: Each agency head must identify regulatory standards that 'may inhibit economic recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic' and may temporarily or permanently rescind, modify, waive, or exempt entities from them.
Agency heads could waive the notice-and-comment requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act while acting under the bill, meaning rules could be changed or scrapped without public input.

Agencies may adopt enforcement-discretion policies declining to enforce against entities that 'attempt in reasonable good faith' to comply, and may not enforce solely because an entity does not adhere to agency guidance.

Agencies must adopt fairness principles in administrative enforcement — including that the government bears the burden of proving violations, penalties must be proportionate, and enforcement must be free of 'unfair surprise' — and must report on which waived rules should be made permanent.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, consumers, patients, and communities who depend on federal rules — workplace safety standards, pollution limits, consumer and financial protections — would bear the risk of suspended or permanently deleted rules. The public would also lose the notice-and-comment opportunity to object before rules changed.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows permanent rescission of regulations while waiving notice and comment, bypassing the public process that normally protects against rules being scrapped without review — and the affected public has no cause of action to challenge it under the bill.

A prohibition on enforcement solely for non-adherence to agency guidance, plus broad enforcement discretion, could weaken oversight of workplace, environmental, and consumer rules precisely when in-person activity resumed during a pandemic.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill: pandemic-era regulatory flexibility (such as eased telehealth rules) did help businesses and patients adapt, and small businesses facing suddenly complex rules had a real argument for forbearance. The bill's savings clause and exceptions for national security, and its sunset no later than the end of the COVID national emergency, put some limits on its reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some temporary regulatory flexibility during a genuine emergency is a legitimate policy tool, and the bill's sponsors pointed to real small-business burdens. But the bill's core mechanism — blanket authority to identify and permanently delete rules without public comment, paired with weakened enforcement — is a broad deregulation grant to regulated industries, with the public bearing the safety and health downside. The narrow sunset limits some damage but does not change the bill's main effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kelly Loeffler introduced the bill on June 11, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party.
No further legislative action was ever taken; the bill never left committee before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing federal health, safety, environmental, consumer, and financial rules remained in force and no rule could be scrapped without public notice and comment. Businesses that hoped for a blanket suspension of regulations gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone relying on existing federal protections

for.name: Sen. Kelly Loeffler
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought referral to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Ron Johnson in the 116th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's only support was its Republican sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses across all sectors (manufacturers, energy, financial firms, large employers)
industries.note: The bill would let them shed or sidestep federal regulatory obligations and face weaker enforcement, with the option of permanent repeal of rules, all without public notice and comment. The compliance-cost savings come directly at the expense of the workplace, environmental, and consumer protections those rules provide.

The bill is framed around giving small businesses confidence to reopen and acknowledges their compliance burdens, and pandemic-era flexibility did help some small firms. But small businesses are also exposed to the weakened safety, consumer, and workplace standards the bill would produce, and the broadest benefits of blanket deregulation tend to accrue to the largest regulated entities.
